id: "bisect_edge"
title: "Halfedge Edge Bisection (bisect_edge)"
category: graphics
requirement: |-
  ## Module: Halfedge Edge Bisection (bisect_edge)
  Split an edge at its midpoint into two sub-edges without touching adjacent faces. Allocates one new vertex (vm), two new halfedges, and one new edge; rewires all twin/next/vertex/edge/face pointers; propagates interpolated corner and bone-weight data via `interpolate_data`. Foundational building block called directly by `split_edge`.

  ## Files to modify

  ## Acceptance signals

=============== catmark_subdivide_helper.yaml ===============
id: "catmark_subdivide_helper"
title: "Catmull-Clark Topological Subdivision Helper (catmark_subdivide_helper)"
category: graphics
requirement: |-
  ## Module: Catmull-Clark Topological Subdivision Helper (catmark_subdivide_helper)
  Perform the full topological Catmull-Clark subdivision of the entire mesh: split every edge (same concept as `split_edge` applied to all edges), split every non-boundary face into quads around a newly-inserted face-center vertex, then update all vertex positions from pre-computed position maps. Called by `catmark_subdivide()` after it computes the new positions.

  ## Files to modify
  - `src/geometry/halfedge-global.cpp`

  ## Acceptance signals
  - `void Halfedge_Mesh::catmark_subdivide_helper(...)`

=============== collapse_edge.yaml ===============
id: "collapse_edge"
title: "Halfedge Edge Collapse (collapse_edge)"
category: graphics
requirement: |-
  ## Module: Halfedge Edge Collapse (collapse_edge)
  Merge the two endpoints of an edge into a single midpoint vertex, removing the edge and adjacent faces that would degenerate. Must detect and reject results that would create a non-manifold mesh, handle both triangle and general polygon faces, and propagate interpolated vertex data via `interpolate_data`.

  ## Files to modify
  - `src/geometry/halfedge-local.cpp`

  ## Acceptance signals
  - `std::optional<Halfedge_Mesh::VertexRef> Halfedge_Mesh::collapse_edge(EdgeRef e)`

=============== extrude_face.yaml ===============
id: "extrude_face"
title: "Halfedge Face Extrusion (extrude_face + extrude_positions)"
category: graphics
requirement: |-
  ## Module: Halfedge Face Extrusion (extrude_face + extrude_positions)
  `extrude_face` creates an inset copy of a face surrounded by new quad side-faces, allocating new vertices, halfedges, edges, and faces. `extrude_positions` then updates those vertex positions by shrinking the inset face toward its centroid and translating it along the face normal by a given distance.

  ## Files to modify
  - `src/geometry/halfedge-local.cpp`

  ## Acceptance signals
  - `std::optional<Halfedge_Mesh::FaceRef> Halfedge_Mesh::extrude_face(FaceRef f)`
  - `void Halfedge_Mesh::extrude_positions(FaceRef face, Vec3 move, float shrink)`

title: "Halfedge Edge Flip (flip_edge)"
category: graphics
requirement: |-
  ## Module: Halfedge Edge Flip (flip_edge)
  Rotate a non-boundary edge CCW within its two containing faces, generalising to arbitrary polygon faces. Rewires halfedge connectivity without allocating new mesh elements, then validates the result is manifold.

  ## Files to modify
  - `src/geometry/halfedge-local.cpp`

  ## Acceptance signals
  - `std::optional<Halfedge_Mesh::EdgeRef> Halfedge_Mesh::flip_edge(EdgeRef e)`

id: "global_mesh_utilities"
title: "Global Mesh Orientation, Normals, and UV Utilities"
category: graphics
requirement: |-
  ## Module: Global Mesh Orientation, Normals, and UV Utilities
  Three independent global mesh utilities:
  - `flip_orientation` reverses all halfedge loop winding to flip face normals.
  - `set_corner_normals` computes per-corner normals using smoothing groups defined by sharp edges and an angle threshold.
  - `set_corner_uvs_per_face` assigns UV coordinates by projecting each face vertex onto a tangent plane perpendicular to the face normal.

  ## Files to modify
  - `src/geometry/halfedge-global.cpp`

  ## Acceptance signals
  - `void Halfedge_Mesh::flip_orientation()`
  - `void Halfedge_Mesh::set_corner_normals(float threshold)`
  - `void Halfedge_Mesh::set_corner_uvs_per_face()`

  ## Files to modify
  - `src/scene/transform.cpp`

  ## Acceptance signals

  - `Mat4 Transform::world_to_local() const`

Calls `bisect_edge` to perform the initial edge bisection, then adds the connecting diagonal half-edges into each adjacent face.

  ## Acceptance signals

Specifications for each function are available in a comment over the declaration. As usual, read carefully! *Complexity Note:* these operations should be work-efficient. This means that their time should generally be linear in the number of mesh elements in a small topological neighborhood of the input. If you find yourself writing code for a local operation that iterates through, e.g., the entire `halfedges` list of the mesh, you are probably doing something wrong. *Robustness Note:* For many local operations there are easy cases (often illustrated below) and hard cases (discuss amongst yourselves!). If your code handles the easy cases correctly and fails gracefully (by not modifying the mesh and returning `std::nullopt`) on the hard cases, you will get 80% of the points for an operation. If your code handles common edge cases "correctly" as well (you can make a sound argument for what the expected output should be), you will receive full points. If you choose to go above and beyond and handle very niche edge cases, we may award extra credit. Please note in your writeup what edge cases you handled. You should aim to implement an operation that performs as you would expect it to - there are countless edge cases for many of these operations that sometimes makes it infeasible to take care of in a timely manner. The goal of this assignment is not to get everything to be "correct," but to implement something that is usable in most scenarios (which will eventually lead to your building of your own model). We've provided an example with `bisect_edge` in the code that can help give an idea on how to proceed with implementing these local operations. ### `A2L1` Flip Edge Given a **non-boundary** edge, rotate it to the vertices one step counterclockwise from its current endpoints. **Note: There is one edge case you should consider accounting for.** ### `A2L2` Split Edge Given an edge, add a vertex in the middle and subdivide adjacent non-boundary faces along the edge from the newly-added vertex to the next-in-ccw-order-from-the-edge vertex in the face. Split edge does not subdivide boundary faces, which is a conceptual thing to make the halfedge data structure complete. A boundary edge's twin's face is a boundary face. You could also simply view boundary faces as the void regions where there is not any "real" faces. All "real" faces of the mesh are non-boundary faces. ### `A2L3` Collapse Edge Merge the two endpoints of an edge at the midpoint of the edge. This will combine all the edges to both endpoints into a new vertex (be careful to not have two edges overlapping). If collapsing the edge would result in an invalid mesh, you should instead do nothing and return `std::nullopt`. Otherwise returns the newly collapsed vertex. It is difficult to restore a mesh after making changes such as deleting data, so you will need to come up with a way to detect these edge cases prior to applying changes to the mesh. **Note: Example of a hard edge case and a simple edge case:** ``` .---.---. . \ / . | | | | \ / | | | | -> | . | (figure 8, and any generalizations of this) | | | | / \ | .---.---. . / \ . ``` ``` . / \ What would a triangle collapse into? / \ .-----. ``` ### `A2L4`, `A2L4h` Extrude Face Extrude face surrounds a face with a ring of quads, so that the face can be moved and/or shrunk by the "extrude positions" helper function. Implementing these two functions will enable the `bevel face` (move a face in the direction of the normal and allow it to expand/shrink) and `extrude face` (move a face in the direction of the normal). Face extrusion is an *incredibly handy* modeling primitive. ## Extra Local Operations You may also implement any of these *optional* local operations for extra credit. You may find that some of them are useful for the global operations below. You will receive extra credit regardless of whether you turn in the operations with A2.0 or A2.5 . Please indicate in your write-up which extra local operations you wish us to grade. ### `A2Lx1` Dissolve Vertex Dissolve vertex removes a vertex by merging all of the adjacent non-boundary faces into one face. Dissolving a vertex on the boundary does not merge with the boundary face. ### `A2Lx2` Dissolve Edge Dissolve edge removes an edge by merging the two adjacent faces into one face. If applied to a boundary edge, the merged face is a boundary. ### `A2Lx3` Collapse Face Collapse face removes a face by shrinking it to a vertex at its center. ### `A2Lx4` Inset Vertex Inset vertex creates a vertex in the middle of a face, and divides the face into triangles around the new vertex. ### `A2Lx5`, `A2Lx5h` Bevel Vertex Bevel vertex replaces a vertex with an (zero-area) face with a vertex for every outgoing edge, ready to be expanded via the bevel positions helper function. Notice that the `bevel_positions` helper function (`A2Lx5h`/`A2Lx6h`) is shared with bevel edge, below. So it might make sense to also do the Bevel Edge task. ### `A2Lx6`, `A2Lx6h` Bevel Edge Bevel edge replaces an edge with an (zero-area) face with a vertex for every outgoing edge, ready to be expanded via the bevel positions helper function. Notice that the `bevel_positions` helper function (`A2Lx5h`/`A2Lx6h`) is shared with bevel vertex, above. Specifications for each function are available in a comment over the declaration. As usual, read carefully! Note that your code need not take special care for non-convex faces (and can, e.g., produce inverted triangles). If you decide to go to the trouble of triangulating non-convex faces in a particularly nice way, call it out in your write-up for potential extra credit. See [Triangulate](A2/triangulate.md) for more information from a previous iteration. ### `A2G2` Linear Subdivision Positions Figure out the correct positions for newly added vertices when doing a Catmull-Clark-style subdivision (without the associated smoothing), so that the mesh remains in the same place. See [Linear Subdivision](A2/linear.md) for more information from a previous iteration. Notice that you are only responsible for computing positions. A helper function exists which actually does the subdivision. ### `A2G3` Catmull-Clark Subdivision Positions Figure out the correct positions for newly added vertices when doing a Catmull-Clark subdivision. Be careful when handling [boundaries](http://15462.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2022/lecture/geometryprocessing/slide_023). See [Catmull-Clark Subdivision](A2/catmull.md) for more information from a previous iteration. Notice that you are only responsible for computing positions. A helper function exists which actually does the subdivision. ## Optional Global Operations (pick one!) To receive full credit on the assignment, you must implement one of the following three operations. Make sure to tell us which one to grade in your write-up. (Others will be graded for extra credit.) ### `A2Go1` Loop Subdivision Subdivide a triangle mesh (a mesh where all non-boundary faces are triangles) using the Loop subdivision rules. Be careful when handling [boundaries](http://15462.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2022/lecture/geometryprocessing/slide_023) (see the Catmull-Clark markdown for a little more clarification). See [Loop Subdivision](A2/loop.md) for more information from a previous iteration. ### `A2Go2` Isotropic Remeshing Produce a mesh with a nicer edge length and angle distribution by repeatedly splitting edges that are too long, collapsing edges that are too short, and applying smoothing (tangent to the surface normal) to vertex positions. See [Isotropic Remeshing](A2/remesh.md) for more information from a previous iteration. **Note: The test cases provided for this task are very basic test cases as the slightly more complicated ones aren't working at the moment. We will grade this operation based off of the GUI and looking at the student's code.** ### `A2Go3` Simplification Produce a mesh with shorter edges by using a quadric error metric to optimally place new vertices. See [Simplification](A2/simplify.md) for more information from a previous iteration. ## Tips Some suggestions which will make your A2 process easier. ### Draw Pictures Meshes are spatial objects. It's hard to reason about them without some sort of visual/spatial representation. When you are trying to figure out how to implement a given operation or debug a problematic case, drawing a picture should be one of your first steps. ### Mesh Validity Given that all of your operations must produce valid meshes as output when run on valid meshes, it's worth understanding what it means for a mesh to be valid. Read the comment above `validate()` in `halfedge.h` and think through the cases that are allowed/disallowed by this specification. The codebase is set up to call `validate()` after every operation. You should not do this in your operation code unless you are debugging, because `validate()` takes time proportional to the size of the mesh, so it breaks the complexity requirements for the local operations.

531	1. **New elements are appended to the live lists.** `halfedge.h:349-351`: `//use emplace_* to allocate new mesh elements: // elements are added at the end of their respective list`. A loop `for (EdgeRef e = edges.begin(); e != edges.end(); ++e)` will therefore also visit the halves you just created (splitting them again → runaway loop / wrong counts); same for `faces` (new quads) and `vertices`. Snapshot first into `std::vector<EdgeRef>` / `std::vector<FaceRef>`. `std::list` iterators stay valid across insertion and across erasure of *other* nodes, so stored `Ref`s are safe. Saving `edges.end()` as a sentinel does **not** work — new nodes are inserted before `end()`.
532	2. **Face corner data must be captured before edge splitting.** After all edges are split, an original face's `next`-cycle has `2d` halfedges alternating old/edge vertices; `f->degree()` returns `2d`, and `f->center()` would average 2d points. Either record each face's corner list / centroid fallback first, or knowingly walk the doubled cycle (`h`, `h->next->next`, …).
533	3. **Positions must be read/derived before any position is written.** Fallback `e->center()` / `f->center()` use `Vertex::position` of the current mesh; if you first write `vertex_positions` into the original vertices, every fallback is computed on the wrong geometry. Compute all new `Vec3`s first, then apply.
534	4. **Erase + emplace aliases addresses, and the maps hash by address.** `emplace_vertex` recycles: `vertices.splice(vertices.end(), free_vertices, free_vertices.begin());` (`halfedge-utility.cpp:56`, same pattern for edges/faces/halfedges), while `erase_*` only splices into the free list — the object keeps its address. `halfedge.h:517-533` hashes `&*key` (`HASH_BY_ADDRESS`). So an erased-then-reallocated element can silently collide with a live key in `vertex_positions`/`edge_vertex_positions`/`face_vertex_positions`, or make a stale `Ref` point at a *different* live element. The clean route is purely additive: reuse the original faces as one of the quads, the original halfedges as the "first halves", and erase nothing.

## 5. Ordering / iteration hazards

1. **New elements are appended to the live lists.** `halfedge.h:349-351`: `//use emplace_* to allocate new mesh elements: // elements are added at the end of their respective list`. A loop `for (EdgeRef e = edges.begin(); e != edges.end(); ++e)` will therefore also visit the halves you just created (splitting them again → runaway loop / wrong counts); same for `faces` (new quads) and `vertices`. Snapshot first into `std::vector<EdgeRef>` / `std::vector<FaceRef>`. `std::list` iterators stay valid across insertion and across erasure of *other* nodes, so stored `Ref`s are safe. Saving `edges.end()` as a sentinel does **not** work — new nodes are inserted before `end()`.
2. **Face corner data must be captured before edge splitting.** After all edges are split, an original face's `next`-cycle has `2d` halfedges alternating old/edge vertices; `f->degree()` returns `2d`, and `f->center()` would average 2d points. Either record each face's corner list / centroid fallback first, or knowingly walk the doubled cycle (`h`, `h->next->next`, …).
3. **Positions must be read/derived before any position is written.** Fallback `e->center()` / `f->center()` use `Vertex::position` of the current mesh; if you first write `vertex_positions` into the original vertices, every fallback is computed on the wrong geometry. Compute all new `Vec3`s first, then apply.
4. **Erase + emplace aliases addresses, and the maps hash by address.** `emplace_vertex` recycles: `vertices.splice(vertices.end(), free_vertices, free_vertices.begin());` (`halfedge-utility.cpp:56`, same pattern for edges/faces/halfedges), while `erase_*` only splices into the free list — the object keeps its address. `halfedge.h:517-533` hashes `&*key` (`HASH_BY_ADDRESS`). So an erased-then-reallocated element can silently collide with a live key in `vertex_positions`/`edge_vertex_positions`/`face_vertex_positions`, or make a stale `Ref` point at a *different* live element. The clean route is purely additive: reuse the original faces as one of the quads, the original halfedges as the "first halves", and erase nothing.
5. **Do not drive topology by iterating the `unordered_map`s.** `/workspace/assignments/A2/halfedge.md:122`: *"neither addresses or the order of iteration of hashed containers (`unordered_*`) will be stable between OS's, standard library versions, or even ... runs of the same program."* Iterate the mesh lists; use the maps only for lookup.

# 1. `void Halfedge_Mesh::flip_orientation()`

Spec (halfedge.h:191–193):

```cpp
	//re-orients every face in the mesh by flipping halfedge directions.
	// no elements are created or erased; only Halfedge::next, Halfedge::vertex, and Vertex::halfedge pointers are changed.
	void flip_orientation();
```

Invoked unconditionally on the whole mesh (widgets.cpp:1113–1117), works on all valid meshes (including boundary loops — "every face").

### Exactly which pointers change
- `Halfedge::next` — every halfedge's, in **every** face **including boundary faces**.
- `Halfedge::vertex` — every halfedge's.
- `Vertex::halfedge` — every vertex's.
- **Unchanged**: `Halfedge::twin`, `Halfedge::edge`, `Halfedge::face`, `Edge::halfedge`, `Face::halfedge`, `Face::boundary`, `Edge::sharp`, all positions, and the element lists themselves (no `emplace_*`/`erase_*`).

### Algorithm
For a face with cycle `h₀ → h₁ → … → h_{n-1} → h₀` where `hᵢ` runs `vᵢ → v_{i+1}`:

1. **Reverse each face's `next` cycle.** `new_next(hᵢ) = old_prev(hᵢ)` (the halfedge whose old `next` was `hᵢ`). Standard implementation: for each face, walk the old cycle collecting `HalfedgeRef`s into a vector, then write `hs[i]->next = hs[(i + hs.size() - 1) % hs.size()]`. Do this for **all** faces in `faces`, boundary included. `Face::halfedge` remains a member of the (reversed) cycle, so it stays valid.
2. **Flip each halfedge's tail vertex.** After reversal `hᵢ` runs `v_{i+1} → vᵢ`, so `new_vertex(hᵢ) = old_vertex(hᵢ->twin) = old_vertex(old_next(hᵢ))`. Because `twin` doesn't move, the cleanest race-free form is to iterate **edges** and swap: `std::swap(e->halfedge->vertex, e->halfedge->twin->vertex)`. (Iterating halfedges and doing `h->vertex = h->twin->vertex` in place is a bug — the second halfedge of the pair reads an already-overwritten value.)
3. **Repoint each vertex.** `v->halfedge = v->halfedge->twin` — if old `h` ran `v → w`, then `h->twin` ran `w → v` and after the flip starts at `v`. This step only reads `Vertex::halfedge` and `twin`, both of which are unaffected by steps 1–2, so its ordering is free. (Equivalently: after step 2, do a pass `for (h) h->vertex->halfedge = h;`.)

This is required by `validate()`, which checks `v->halfedge->vertex == v`, that `face->halfedge(->next)^n` is a cycle containing exactly the halfedges referencing that face, and that `vertex->halfedge(->twin->next)^n` is a cycle (halfedge-utility.cpp l. 587–617). The vertex orbit direction (`h->twin->next`) reverses as a side effect — that's expected and legal.

`flip_orientation()` must be an exact involution: calling it twice restores the original mesh bit-for-bit.

### Corner data
The header sentence *"only `Halfedge::next`, `Halfedge::vertex`, and `Vertex::halfedge` pointers are changed"* is the spec, and it says nothing about `corner_uv`/`corner_normal`. **The literal, minimal, and most defensible implementation leaves both untouched.** That is also self-consistent (still an involution) and cannot break `validate()`.

Be aware of the semantic wrinkle, and mention it in a comment: a halfedge's corner data describes the corner **at `h->vertex`** (see indexed.cpp l. 18–22, `vert.pos = h->vertex->position; vert.norm = h->corner_normal; vert.uv = h->corner_uv;`, and model.cpp:474). Since `h->vertex` moves one step around the face, leaving the data in place rotates the per-face UV/normal assignment by one corner. If you want appearance to be preserved, the corresponding transport is `h->corner_* = old_next(h)->corner_*` (data moves one corner backwards, since `new_vertex(h) == old_vertex(old_next(h))`), with `corner_normal` **negated** because the surface orientation reversed. Both variants are involutions. I recommend implementing the literal one (no data changes) since that matches the header, and noting that users are expected to re-run "Smooth Normals" after flipping.

### Sibling to imitate (exact code, halfedge-global.cpp:331–346)

```cpp
void Halfedge_Mesh::set_corner_uvs_project(Vec3 origin, Vec3 u_axis, Vec3 v_axis) {

	u_axis /= u_axis.norm_squared();
	v_axis /= v_axis.norm_squared();

	for (auto &halfedge : halfedges) {
		if (halfedge.face->boundary) {
			halfedge.corner_uv = Vec2(0.0f, 0.0f);
		} else {
			halfedge.corner_uv = Vec2(
				dot(halfedge.vertex->position - origin, u_axis),
				dot(halfedge.vertex->position - origin, v_axis)
			);
		}
	}
}
```

### Derived exact behaviour
I reverse-engineered this from the two reference files and **verified numerically that the rule below reproduces every stored UV with error exactly 0.0** on all 7 non-boundary faces of `uv-cube.js3d` (6 faces) and `uv-plane.js3d` (1 face):

For each **non-boundary** face `f`:

1. `Vec3 n = f.normal();` (the unit Newell normal already provided by `Face::normal()`).
2. Build a right-handed tangent frame `(u_axis, v_axis, n)` with **`cross(u_axis, v_axis) == n`**:
   - `u_axis` = a fixed world axis projected into the face plane and normalized: `a - dot(a, n) * n`, normalized;
   - `a = Vec3(0,0,1)` normally; when `n` is parallel to `+z`/`-z` (projection degenerate), fall back to `a = Vec3(0,1,0)`.
   - `v_axis = cross(n, u_axis);`
   
   Equivalently and more robustly, pick `a` as the coordinate axis with the smallest `|dot(a, n)|`, breaking ties toward the *later* axis (x < y < z). **Both formulations reproduce the reference data bit-exactly**; the data (all normals axis-aligned) cannot distinguish them. Observed frames: `n=(0,0,±1)→u=(0,1,0)`; `n=(±1,0,0)` and `n=(0,±1,0)→u=(0,0,1)`; `v` always `= cross(n,u)`.
3. Compute `U = dot(p, u_axis)`, `V = dot(p, v_axis)` for each corner position `p = h->vertex->position`; take the face's min/max of each.
4. **Normalize the face's tangent-plane bounding box onto the full unit square**: `corner_uv = Vec2((U - Umin) / (Umax - Umin), (V - Vmin) / (Vmax - Vmin))`. Guard a zero extent (degenerate/collinear face) with e.g. `extent = 1.0f` or output `0.5f`, otherwise you write NaN and `validate()` fails at halfedge-utility.cpp:476–477.

**Scale/offset answer:** there is no world-space scale — the scale is *per face*, `1/extent` along each tangent axis, with offset `-min/extent`. **What a unit square maps to:** the *whole* texture (the unit square in UV space) maps onto *each* face's tangent-plane bounding rectangle — every face gets exactly one complete, axis-aligned copy of the texture, with `(0,0)` at the min-u/min-v corner and `(1,1)` at the max-u/max-v corner. For `cube(r)` this makes each 2r×2r face span exactly `[0,1]²`, confirmed by `uv-cube.js3d`.

Two normalizations are consistent with the data (all reference faces are squares): per-axis bbox (above) and a single uniform scale by the larger extent. Per-axis bbox is the right reading of "map texture per-face" (each face shows the entire texture, no letterboxing); use it.

**Boundary halfedges:** `corner_uv = Vec2(0.0f, 0.0f)`, exactly as `set_corner_uvs_project` does. Confirmed by `uv-plane.js3d`, whose 4 boundary-loop halfedges all store `(0,0)` while the single interior quad carries a full per-face mapping.
